In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the saying/implicating distinction has been shown to be a false dichotomy, and that there are no grounds to retain the notion of ‘what was said’.
there is no such thing as ‘what is said’, and the saying/implicating distinction is not a useful one.

‘what is said’, if such a notion is needed at all, should be equated with explicature, and that explicature should be understood as a pragmatic enrichment of the context-free semantic content of an expression type.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the distinction between saying and implying is a distinction of the type of communicated assumption, and not of the type of assumption.
the notion of ‘what-is-said’ is not necessary to explain how language is used to communicate.
the distinction between saying and implying is a pragmatic one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the notion of ‘what a sentence says’ is redundant, since it is subsumed by the notion of explicature.
the saying/implicating distinction should be replaced with an explicature/implicative distinction.
the saying/implicating distinction is not a distinction between two types of communicated assumptions, but a distinction between two kinds of pragmatic development of encoded meaning.
